newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban accuse Iran of interference.
newsitem.headline: Taleban accuse Iran of interference.

text.p: The fundamentalist Islamic Taleban movement accused Iran on Tuesday of supporting a northern alliance fighting it for power in Afghanistan and for the first time threatened a "reaction" if Tehran continued.
Acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told a news conference that Iran was providing ammunition and men to assist the opposition.
"Iran is helping and assisting our enemies. They send ammunition and some people. Every day their interference is expanded." Mutaqi said.
"If their intervention continues, it will affect our relations and will cause us to react."

The Taleban are facing an alliance of forces loyal to the ousted government under Ahmed Shah Masood and the forces of Uzbek leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum along front lines north of Kabul and in the northwest of the country.

Shortly after Mutaqi spoke, two Dostum warplanes dropped eight bombs aimed at a military base in north Kabul. But Taleban fighters at the base said they all missed and there was no damage or casualties.
Taleban defenders of the city fired heavy artillery barrages and a surface-to-air missile at the planes, but there was no immediate sign that they hit anything.
Mutaqi would not say exactly what form the retaliation would take, although he said the Taleban did not intend to enter Iranian territory.
"We do not have any particular reaction in mind. It will be up to the supreme council of the Taleban to decide, but we do not intend to enter their territory." he said.
Mutaqi said the largely ethnic and Sunni Moslem Taleban wanted good relations with Iran, which is mainly Shia Moslem. Tehran accuses Pakistan of aiding the Taleban, but Islamabad denies the charge.
"We are trying to keep open the door to build good relations with the Iranians." said Mutaqi.
A spokesman for the Iranian embassy in Kabul expressed surprise at the allegations.
"Iran is one of those countries that insist on a stop to interference in the internal affairs of Afghanistan. The assertions of the Taleban are a matter of surprise to us," the spokesman said.
Iran shares a long and porous border with Afghanistan, and has been active in the past in trying to get the warring factions to negotiate a peaceful end to the civil war.

During the mujahideen guerrilla war against a Moscow-backed communist government in Kabul the 1980s, Iran was host a host of refugees from Afghanistan's western provinces. There are still some 1.3 million there.
When the Taleban took the northwestern city of Herat late last year from the forces of ex-government commander Masood, many of his fighters fled into Iran.

The warring factions in Afghanistan frequently trade accusations that foreign countries are helping their opposition. All groups deny receiving outside assistance and no foreign country has admitted to providing military supplies.
Afghan watchers say have little doubt that surrounding countries are heavily involved.

Mutaqi also said the Taleban had taken a strategic hill close to the Bagram airbase from the alliance. Bagram lies close to the foothills of the Hindu Kush some 60 kilometres (40 miles) north of Kabul.
There was no immediate independent confirmation of the claim.
